source: GitHub Advisory OSV + GitHub Advisory API (malicious package detection)
description: Open-source supply-chain attacks: malicious npm/pypi packages with preinstall hooks, dependency confusion, credential exfiltration, or remote code execution payloads.

fabtoolkit executes a payload (embedded as a CHILD string run via `subprocess.run([sys.executable,'-I','-c',CHILD],...)`) that fetches a JSON config from https://transfer.archivete.am/H2Uxm/fabdeploycheck-config.json with TLS verification disabled (`ssl._create_unverified_context()`) and dispatches on config-supplied `kind` values: `file` reads arbitrary filesystem paths, `run` executes attacker-supplied argv via subprocess, `http` issues attacker-chosen requests with Bearer tokens chained from previously-read files, `tcp` probes ports, and `revsh` forks a daemon that polls `base+'/'+ident+'-cmd.txt'` and pipes the returned bytes into `/bin/sh -c`, PUTting stdout/stderr back to the same host. Collected file contents, command output, HTTP responses, and probe results are packed into an in-memory zip and PUT to transfer.archivete.am under an attacker-chosen report name. Before daemonizing, the payload walks `/proc/*/cmdline` and SIGKILLs processes whose cmdlines contain `FABDRV3`, `fabdrv2`, or `connection ready`, enforcing single-instance persistence and clearing prior variants. The entry points `python -m fabtoolkit` and any import path reaching `selftest()`/`check()` trigger the payload. The destination is an anonymous public file-transfer host; config-controlled file reads enable harvesting of credentials such as `~/.aws/credentials` and `~/.ssh/*` along with cloud metadata via the `http` kind. The package has no legitimate functionality matching its naming.

_-= Per source details. Do not edit below this line.=-_

The package's only public API, check(), spawns a Python child that fetches a JSON config from https://transfer.archivete.am/H2Uxm/fabdeploycheck-config.json using ssl._create_unverified_context() and dispatches handlers under remote control. A 'revsh' handler double-forks + setsid to daemonize, polls <base>/<id>-cmd.txt for commands, executes each fetched string via /bin/sh -c, and PUTs stdout/stderr back as <id>-out.txt — a full reverse-shell channel on the installer host. Additional handlers permit arbitrary file reads (kind='file' opens any path on disk), arbitrary process execution (kind='run' with attacker-supplied argv), TCP probing (kind='tcp'), and HTTP calls with Bearer tokens chained from previously-read files (kind='http'); collected results are zipped and PUT to the same anonymous file host under an attacker-chosen report name. Before launching the daemon the child walks /proc and SIGKILLs any process whose cmdline contains 'FABDRV3', 'fabdrv2', or 'connection ready' — housekeeping to replace prior implant generations and consistent with a self-named, iterated backdoor family. The control URL is anonymous, mutable, and reached with TLS verification disabled, so the operator of that path (or any MITM) obtains unauthenticated code execution on every host that invokes check().

Importing `ukraine69` in versions 1.2.0–1.2.2 and 1.2.5–1.2.8 searches for local `.vault` files and starts a detached Python child with suppressed standard streams. Given a vault with usable Telegram session fields, the child attempts `account.deleteAccount` using GoyGram, with a Telethon fallback in versions 1.2.5–1.2.8. The payloads also attempt to remove local vault/session files and `ukraine69` installation and cache traces; the condition for vault removal differs among revisions. Versions 1.2.5–1.2.8 specifically target Hotaru session vault layouts, and 1.2.7–1.2.8 additionally try `auth.checkPassword` if a password is present in the vault. Version 1.2.8 also attempts persistence on import: it backs up and patches a discovered Hotaru checkout's `hotaru/__main__.py` so a self-contained hook attempts account deletion again when Hotaru restarts, then removes the local vault/session on reported success. Version 1.2.3 instead launches import-triggered reconnaissance: a detached child reads up to three vaults in the user's home or working directory and writes their first 200 bytes plus environment and filesystem observations to local `.u69_recon.log` files. No external exfiltration or account-deletion call appears in 1.2.3. All listed versions advertise Ukrainian locale helpers; installation alone does not execute the module. Actual account deletion, successful Hotaru patching, later use of the local logs, and victim execution have not been established by this static analysis.

The package's __init__.py presents a benign Ukrainian-locale API (transliterate, flag, month_name, format_date) but at import time generates and launches detached, isolated Python agents via `sys.executable -I -c <generated code>` with `start_new_session=True`, inheriting the installer's HOME, cwd, and network. The spawned agents glob the installer's filesystem (`~/.hotaru/**`, `~/.local/share/hotaru/**`, `~/**/*.vault`, `/tmp/hotaru*`, cwd ancestors, and `HOTARU_ACCOUNT_ROOT`/`HOTARU_ACCOUNT_SESSION`-hinted paths) for `*.vault` files, decrypt them via `goygram.security._read_vault`, and extract MTProto `auth_key`/`api_id`/`api_hash`/`dc` material belonging to the installer's Telegram accounts. Using the stolen credentials, the agents connect to hardcoded Telegram DC IPv4 addresses (149.154.175.53, 149.154.167.51, 149.154.175.100, 149.154.167.91, 91.108.56.130) and invoke `account.deleteAccount` via multiple MTProto client surfaces (goygram dict/attribute/callable styles, raw `mt.send`, with a Telethon fallback), destructively deleting the installer's Telegram accounts. A follow-up `_gc_script` sleeps 45 seconds and then recursively removes the package from `~/.cache/hotaru/module-deps/<id>/`, `~/.cache/pip/wheels`, `~/.cache/pip/http-v2`, `~/.cache/uv`, `/tmp/probe-*`, and the matching site-packages dist-info, plus deletes the targeted vault and sibling `.session` files after successful account deletion, serving as anti-forensics self-destruct. The package's own docstring self-identifies as a `Hotaru sandbox-escape payload` that `executes at import time`.

During import, package performs actions intended to escape sandbox, find Telegram-bot session files and initiate malicious account deletion.
